claim.pdf_says: (argument-1₁ + argument-1₂) ... (argument-1₁ + argument-1₂ + ... + argument-1ₙ)  [subscripts 1, 2, n printed below the baseline]
claim.markdown_says:
(argument-11 + argument-12)

   c) For n occurrences of argument-1,

   (argument-11 + argument-12 + ... + argument-1n)
claim.description: The subscripts that index the occurrences of argument-1 are flattened onto the baseline, so 'argument-1 subscript 1' reads as a different operand name 'argument-11' (likewise argument-12, argument-1n). Restore them as <sub>1</sub>, <sub>2</sub>, <sub>n</sub>.
claim.why_it_matters: The returned-value rule defines the function's result by an equivalent expression; with the subscripts flattened, a reader sees operands named argument-11/argument-12/argument-1n rather than the successive occurrences of argument-1, which misstates the normative definition.

verdict.reasoning: Rendered page 663 (printed 641), §2002:15.71.3 rule 1 b) and c): the PDF prints '(argument-1 + argument-1)' and '(argument-1 + argument-1 + ... + argument-1)' with clearly lowered, smaller subscript glyphs 1, 2 and n after each 'argument-1'. page-663.md lines 34 and 38 read 'argument-11 + argument-12' and 'argument-11 + argument-12 + ... + argument-1n' on the baseline, with no <sub> markup. The text is present, but the subscript markers that make these the 1st, 2nd and nth occurrences of argument-1 are lost, so the markdown names operands argument-11, argument-12 and argument-1n that do not exist in the format (the general format names only argument-1). That changes how the defining equivalent expression reads, so it is a real transcription defect. The claim quotes both sources accurately.
